cards.b:
Every cell is wrapped in a membrane that decides what enters and leaves, like a gate with a guard. If it fails, the cell dies. Salt balance, nerve signals, drug action and even why a pickled mango stays dry all depend on membranes.

The membrane is selective: oxygen and small fatty molecules slip through, while ions and large molecules need special doors. Think of a railway station with ticket gates, where only passengers with the right ticket enter. Salting raw mango works because water leaves the fruit cells by osmosis. A membrane is about 7 nanometres thick, thousands of times thinner than a hair.

In 1972 S.J. Singer and Garth Nicolson proposed the fluid mosaic model. The membrane is a double layer of phospholipids. Each has a water-loving head and two water-fearing tails. Tails hide inside, heads face water on both sides. Proteins float in it like boats on a sea, and cholesterol adjusts fluidity.

Molecules move from high to low concentration. This is diffusion. Small non-polar molecules like oxygen slip straight through. Water moves by osmosis, often through channels called aquaporins (Peter Agre, Nobel 2003). Large or charged molecules use facilitated diffusion through channel or carrier proteins.

Moving things uphill, from low to high, needs ATP. The sodium-potassium pump pushes 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP. Jens Skou discovered it (Nobel 1997). It keeps nerve cells ready to fire and drives much of your energy use.

Think of it as a pump hauling water uphill: it needs fuel. The pump changes shape after taking a phosphate from ATP, releasing sodium outside, then grabbing potassium and flipping back. Because it keeps more Na+ outside and more K+ inside, the cell stores an electrical charge, like a charged battery. Nerves and muscles use that stored charge to fire signals.

Water moves toward the saltier side. Put a raisin in water: it swells. Salt on a slug or on pickles pulls water out. Plant cells in fresh water become firm (turgid); in strong salt they shrink (plasmolysis).

Large particles cross inside bubbles. Endocytosis brings material in (phagocytosis means 'cell eating', pinocytosis 'cell drinking'). Exocytosis sends material out, as when nerve cells release signals.

Steps of endocytosis: the membrane dents inward around the particle, pinches off as a bubble called a vesicle, and carries it inside. In exocytosis the reverse happens, and a vesicle fuses with the outer membrane and empties outside, like posting a parcel. White blood cells use phagocytosis to swallow bacteria. Insulin is released from pancreas cells by exocytosis. Both processes need ATP.

Remember it as a delivery van: cargo goes in the van, not through the wall.

Ernest Overton (1890s) noticed that fat-soluble substances enter cells easily, hinting at a fatty membrane. In 1925 Gorter and Grendel extracted lipids from red blood cells and found enough to cover the cells twice, suggesting a double layer.

The Gorter and Grendel result is an old but neat piece of reasoning: if the lipids covered twice the cell surface, the membrane must be two layers thick. Their numbers were a little off, though the conclusion held. In 1935 Danielli and Davson added proteins to the picture, and in 1972 Singer and Nicolson proposed the fluid mosaic model, where proteins float in a sea of lipids.

Correct this

  • Osmosis is movement of water, not salt.
  • The membrane is not a rigid wall; it flows.
  • Active transport is not always faster; it is about direction against the gradient.

One more: diffusion is not a pull by the cell. Molecules simply spread from crowded to empty regions through random motion, like the smell of cooking drifting across a house, and this needs no energy.

Cells keep their shape because water balance is controlled: a cell in very salty water shrinks, and one in pure water swells and can burst if it has no wall.

During cholera epidemics, Indian-origin doctors like Dilip Mahalanabis used oral rehydration solution during the 1971 refugee crisis. It works because glucose helps sodium enter gut cells through a carrier, and water follows by osmosis. It has saved millions of children.

Mahalanabis worked with refugees near the Bangladesh border, where IV fluid ran short, and he used a salt and glucose drink instead; deaths from cholera fell sharply. The Lancet later called ORS potentially the most important medical advance of the 20th century. A simple home version uses clean water, a pinch of salt and sugar.

• Membrane: phospholipid bilayer with proteins (fluid mosaic, 1972).
  • Passive: diffusion, osmosis, facilitated.
  • Active: needs ATP, goes against gradient.
  • Bulk: endocytosis and exocytosis.

Think about it:

  1. Why does adding salt to a wound sting or dry a leech?
  2. Why does ORS need both sugar and salt?
